title: How Tarot Works?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history of tarot, debunking the myth that playing cards evolved from tarot. They trace playing cards from China through the Mamluk Empire in Egypt to Italy, where tarot began as a trick-taking game (tarocco) around the 15th century. They then cover how Antoine Court de Gébelin and Louis Raphaël de Fabre d'Olivet invented the divination use in the 1780s, linking it falsely to the Book of Thoth; later occultists (Éliphas Lévi, Paul Christian, Aleister Crowley, A. E. Waite) added mythology. The Waite-Smith deck (1909, illustrated by Pamela Colman Smith) became the most popular. They explain the major and minor arcana, notable cards (Tower, Ten of Swords, Fool, Death, Moon), spreads like the Celtic Cross, cartomancy, Carl Jung's interest, and scientific explanations for accurate readings (cold reading, Forer/Barnum effect). Listener mail issues a correction about John Denver's toxicology report.

entities.name: Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn
The Pictorial Key to the Tarot

segments.title: Opening banter and tarot's current popularity
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode and talks about tarot's recent popularity, including his wife Emily's morning tarot habit and sales figures.

segments.title: Playing cards predate tarot and the Mamluk connection
segments.summary: The hosts debunk the myth that playing cards evolved from tarot, tracing playing cards to China in the thirteenth century, then to Egypt under the Mamluk Empire, where polo sticks were a suit.

segments.title: Tarot as a trick-taking game in Italy
segments.summary: Playing cards reached Italy, where tarot was created as a game with twenty-two added trump cards, giving rise to trick-taking games. The name changed from tarocchi to taroc, and later spread to France.

segments.title: Tarot divination invented by Antoine Court de Gébelin
segments.summary: The hosts explain that tarot's divination use is recent and was invented by Antoine Court de Gébelin, who made up esoteric claims in his writings, and distinguish tarot from cartomancy.

segments.title: Gébelin's collaborator, the Book of Thoth claim, and a tangent
segments.summary: Gébelin and Louis de Fabre d'Olivet linked the cards to the Book of Thoth. The hosts digress briefly into a discussion of the Ghostbusters films.

segments.title: Later occultists and the Waite-Smith deck
segments.summary: Occultists including Éliphas Lévi, Paul Christian, and Aleister Crowley added fanciful mythology. A. E. Waite's 1910 Pictorial Key to the Tarot, illustrated by Pamela Colman Smith, produced the Waite-Smith deck, now the most popular.

segments.title: Deck structure and notable cards
segments.summary: The hosts describe the seventy-eight cards: fifty-six minor arcana in four suits and twenty-two major arcana. They discuss the Tower, Ten of Swords, Fool, Death, and Moon cards and how upright and reversed positions affect meaning.

segments.title: Spreads, readings, and psychotherapy uses
segments.summary: The hosts cover spreads such as the three-card and Celtic Cross, reading etiquette, and Carl Jung's interest in tarot, with some psychotherapists using it as a reflection tool.

segments.title: Scientific explanations: cold reading and the Forer effect
segments.summary: Accurate readings are explained by cold reading and the Forer (Barnum) effect, where people accept generic statements as personal and remember hits over misses.

segments.title: Listener mail correction on John Denver
segments.summary: A listener letter from John Denver's family says toxicology tests were negative for drugs in the 1997 crash; Josh apologizes for the earlier false claim. A West Virginia versus Virginia feud is briefly mentioned.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing remarks and contact information for listener mail.
